paragraphs: Father Païssy was not wrong, of course, when he decided that his “dear boy” would come back. Perhaps he even saw, to some extent, what Alyosha’s spiritual state really meant. Still, I must admit frankly that it would be very hard for me to give a clear account of that strange, vague time in the life of the young hero I love so much. Father Païssy asked sorrowfully, “Are you too with those of little faith?” I could of course answer confidently for Alyosha, “No, he is not with those of little faith. Quite the opposite.” In fact, all his trouble came from having great faith. But the trouble was there all the same, and it was so agonizing that even long afterwards Alyosha thought of that sorrowful day as one of the bitterest and most fatal of his life. Suppose someone asks: “Could all his grief and turmoil really have come only from the fact that his elder’s body had shown signs of early decay, instead of working miracles at once?” I must answer without beating about the bush, “Yes, it certainly could.” I only ask the reader not to be in too great a hurry to laugh at my young hero’s pure heart. I am far from wanting to apologize for him, or to defend his innocent faith on the grounds of his youth, or the little he had studied, or any such reason. On the contrary, I declare that I have real respect for the qualities of his heart. No doubt a youth who took in impressions cautiously, whose love was lukewarm, and whose mind was too prudent for his age and so of little value, might, I admit, have avoided what happened to my hero. But in some cases it does more credit to a man to be carried away by an emotion, however unreasonable, that springs from great love, than to stay unmoved. And this is even truer in youth, because a young man who is always sensible is to be distrusted and is worth little—that’s my opinion!
“But,” reasonable people will perhaps exclaim, “not every young man can believe in such a superstition, and your hero is no model for others.”
To this I answer again, “Yes! My hero had faith, a faith holy and steadfast, but still I am not going to apologize for him.”

I said above, and perhaps too hastily, that I would not explain or justify my hero. But I see that some explanation is needed if the rest of my story is to be understood. So let me say this: it was not a question of miracles. There was no frivolous, impatient expectation of miracles in his mind. And Alyosha did not need miracles at that moment to prove some preconceived idea—oh, no, not at all. What he saw before everything was one figure—the figure of his beloved elder, that holy man whom he revered with such adoration. The fact is that all the love hidden in his pure young heart for everyone and everything had, for the past year, been concentrated—perhaps wrongly—on one person, his beloved elder. It is true that he had accepted this person for so long as his ideal that all his young strength and energy could not help turning toward that ideal, even to the point of forgetting, for the moment, “everyone and everything.” Afterwards he remembered that on that terrible day he had completely forgotten his brother Dmitri, about whom he had been so anxious and troubled the day before. He had forgotten, too, to take the two hundred roubles to Ilusha’s father, though he had so warmly meant to do it the evening before. But again, it was not miracles he needed, only “the higher justice,” which, as he believed, had been outraged by the blow that had so suddenly and cruelly wounded his heart. And what does it matter that this “justice” Alyosha looked for inevitably took the shape of miracles to be worked at once by the ashes of his adored teacher? Why, everyone in the monastery cherished the same thought and the same hope, even those whose intellects Alyosha respected, Father Païssy himself, for instance. And so Alyosha, with no doubts to trouble him, dressed his dreams in the same form as all the rest. A whole year of life in the monastery had made this expectation a habit in his heart. But it was justice, justice, that he thirsted for, not simply miracles.

And now the man who, he believed, should have been raised above everyone in the whole world, that man, instead of receiving the glory that was his due, was suddenly disgraced and dishonored! What for? Who had judged him? Who could have decreed this? These were the questions that tormented his inexperienced, untouched heart. He could not bear without mortification, even resentment, that the holiest of holy men should have been exposed to the jeering, spiteful mockery of a frivolous crowd so far beneath him. Even if there had been no miracles, even if there had been nothing marvelous to justify his hopes, why this insult, why this humiliation, why this early decay, “in excess of nature,” as the spiteful monks said? Why this “sign from heaven,” which they so triumphantly welcomed along with Father Ferapont, and why did they think they had won the right to welcome it? Where is the finger of Providence? Why did Providence hide its face “at the most critical moment” (so Alyosha thought it), as though it chose to submit to the blind, dumb, pitiless laws of nature?

That was why Alyosha’s heart was bleeding. And of course, as I have said already, the sting of it all was that the man he loved above everything on earth should be shamed and humiliated! This murmuring may have been shallow and unreasonable in my hero, but I say again for the third time—and I am ready to admit that my feeling may be hard to defend—that I am glad he showed himself not too reasonable at that moment. Any sensible man will come back to reason in time, but if love does not get the upper hand in a boy’s heart at such an exceptional moment, when will it? I will not, however, leave out something strange that came to the surface of Alyosha’s mind for a time, in this fatal and confused moment. This new something was the harassing impression left by the conversation with Ivan, which now haunted Alyosha’s mind again and again. At this moment it haunted him. Oh, it was not that something of the fundamental, elemental, so to speak, faith of his soul had been shaken. He loved his God and believed in Him steadfastly, though he was suddenly murmuring against Him. Still, a vague but tormenting and evil impression left by his conversation with Ivan the day before suddenly revived in his soul and seemed to be forcing its way up into his consciousness.

It was beginning to get dark when Rakitin, crossing the pine copse from the hermitage to the monastery, suddenly noticed Alyosha. He was lying face down on the ground under a tree, not moving, apparently asleep. Rakitin went up and called him by name.
“You here, Alexey? Can you have—” he began in surprise, but broke off. He had meant to say, “Can you have come to this?”
Alyosha did not look at him, but from a slight movement Rakitin saw at once that he heard and understood.
“What’s the matter?” he went on; but the surprise on his face slowly turned into a smile that grew more and more ironical.
“Listen, I’ve been looking for you for the last two hours. You suddenly vanished. What are you up to? What kind of foolery is this? You might at least look at me...”

Alyosha raised his head, sat up and leaned his back against the tree. He was not crying, but his face looked pained and irritable. He did not look at Rakitin, though; he looked away to one side of him.
“Do you know your face has completely changed? There’s none of your famous mildness left in it. Are you angry with someone? Have they been mistreating you?”
“Leave me alone,” said Alyosha suddenly, with a weary wave of his hand, still looking away from him.

“Oho! So that’s how we’re feeling! So you can shout at people like the rest of us mortals. That’s a come-down from the angels. Listen, Alyosha, you’ve surprised me, do you hear? I mean it. It’s a long time since anything here surprised me. I always took you for an educated man....”
Alyosha finally looked at him, but vaguely, as though he hardly understood what Rakitin said.
“Can you really be so upset just because your old man has started to stink? You don’t mean to say you seriously believed he was going to work miracles?” exclaimed Rakitin, genuinely surprised again.
“I believed, I believe, I want to believe, and I will believe, what more do you want?” cried Alyosha irritably.

“Nothing at all, my boy. Damn it all! Why, no schoolboy of thirteen believes in that now. But there.... So now you’re in a temper with your God, you’re rebelling against Him; He hasn’t given you a promotion, He hasn’t handed out the medal of merit! Eh, what a bunch you are!”
Alyosha gazed for a long while at Rakitin with his eyes half closed, and a sudden gleam came into them ... but not a gleam of anger at Rakitin.
“I am not rebelling against my God; I simply ‘don’t accept His world.’” Alyosha suddenly gave a forced smile.
“What do you mean, you don’t accept the world?” Rakitin thought a moment over his answer. “What idiocy is this?”
Alyosha did not answer.
“Come on, enough nonsense, now to business. Have you had anything to eat today?”
“I don’t remember.... I think I have.”

“You need building up, to judge by your face. It makes a man sorry to look at you. You didn’t sleep all night either, I hear; you had a meeting in there. And then all this fuss afterwards. Most likely you’ve had nothing to eat but a mouthful of holy bread. I’ve got some sausage in my pocket; I brought it from the town in case of need, only you won’t eat sausage....”
“Give me some.”

“Well, well! You’re going it! Why, it’s a regular mutiny, with barricades! Right, my boy, we must make the most of it. Come to my place.... I wouldn’t mind a drop of vodka myself, I’m tired to death. Vodka is going too far for you, I suppose ... or would you like some?”
“Give me some vodka too.”
“Hello! You surprise me, brother!” Rakitin looked at him in amazement. “Well, one way or another, vodka or sausage, this is a damned fine chance and mustn’t be missed. Come along.”
Alyosha got up in silence and followed Rakitin.
“If your little brother Ivan could see this—wouldn’t he be surprised! By the way, your brother Ivan set off for Moscow this morning, did you know?”

“Yes,” answered Alyosha listlessly, and suddenly the image of his brother Dmitri rose before his mind. But only for a minute. It reminded him of something that must not be put off for a moment, some duty, some terrible obligation, yet even that reminder made no impression on him. It did not reach his heart, and it faded out of his mind at once and was forgotten. But, a long while afterwards, Alyosha remembered this.

“Your brother Ivan once declared that I was a ‘liberal booby with no talents whatsoever.’ Once you, too, couldn’t resist letting me know I was ‘dishonorable.’ Well! I’d like to see what your talents and sense of honor will do for you now.” Rakitin finished this speech to himself in a whisper.

“Listen!” he said aloud, “let’s take the path beyond the monastery, straight to the town. Hm! I ought to stop at Madame Hohlakov’s on the way. Just imagine, I wrote to tell her everything that happened, and would you believe it, she answered me right away in pencil (the lady has a passion for writing notes) that ‘she would never have expected _such conduct_ from a man of such a reverend character as Father Zossima.’ That was her very word: ‘conduct.’ She’s angry too. Eh, what a bunch you are! Wait!” he cried suddenly. He stopped short and, taking Alyosha by the shoulder, made him stop too.

“Do you know, Alyosha,” he peeped inquisitively into his eyes. A new thought had suddenly dawned on him, and though he was laughing outwardly, he was plainly afraid to say it aloud, so hard did he still find it to believe in the strange, unexpected mood in which he now saw Alyosha. “Alyosha, do you know where we had better go?” he brought out at last, timidly and insinuatingly.
“I don’t care ... wherever you like.”
“Let’s go to Grushenka, eh? Will you come?” said Rakitin at last, trembling with timid suspense.
“Let’s go to Grushenka,” Alyosha answered calmly, at once, and this prompt, calm agreement surprised Rakitin so much that he almost jumped back.
“Well! Listen to that!” he cried in amazement, but he seized Alyosha firmly by the arm and led him along the path, still afraid he would change his mind.
They walked along in silence; Rakitin was positively afraid to talk.

“And how glad she’ll be, how delighted!” he muttered, but fell silent again. And in fact it was not to please Grushenka that he was taking Alyosha to her. He was a practical person and never undertook anything without a prospect of gain for himself. His aim in this case was twofold. First, he wanted revenge: he wished to see “the downfall of the righteous,” Alyosha’s fall “from the saints to the sinners,” and he was already gloating over it in his imagination. Second, he had in view a certain material gain for himself, of which more will be said later.
“So the critical moment has come,” he thought to himself with spiteful glee, “and we’ll catch it on the hop, for it’s just what we want.”
